lessons.title: Common Turkey Diseases
lessons.body: Turkeys in Africa face several diseases that can wipe out your flock quickly if you don't act fast. The most common is Newcastle disease, which causes sneezing, coughing, twisting of the neck, and sudden death. It spreads through droppings, contaminated feed, and even your shoes. There is no cure, so vaccination is your only protection. Another killer is fowl pox, which shows as scabs on the head, legs, and mouth. It spreads slowly but can kill young poults. Blackhead disease is a big problem where turkeys share space with chickens. It causes yellow droppings, drooping wings, and darkening of the head. Chickens carry the parasite but don't get sick, so never keep turkeys and chickens together. Coccidiosis is caused by a tiny parasite in dirty water and wet litter. It leads to bloody droppings and weakness. Treat with amprolium in drinking water for 5 days. CRD (chronic respiratory disease) causes rattling breath and swollen eyes; use tylosin or doxycycline as directed by a vet. To prevent these, keep your turkey house dry, clean feeders daily, and isolate any new birds for 3 weeks. In Africa, many farmers lose birds because they don't recognize early signs. Check your flock every morning: look for birds that stand apart, have pale combs, or refuse to eat. If you see these signs, call a vet or agricultural extension officer immediately. Remember, dead birds should be buried deep or burned, never eaten or sold. With good management, you can reduce disease outbreaks by up to 80%.

lessons.title: Vaccination Protocols
lessons.body: Vaccination is the cheapest insurance for your turkeys. In Africa, the most important vaccines are for Newcastle disease (ND), fowl pox, and sometimes fowl typhoid. Start with ND vaccine at day 1 for poults, given as a drop in the eye or nostril. Repeat at 3 weeks and again at 8 weeks. After that, booster every 3 months if you keep breeders. For fowl pox, vaccinate at 4 weeks by wing web stab. Use a two-pronged needle to prick the wing web; check for scabs 7-10 days later to confirm it worked. Store vaccines in a cooler with ice packs, never in direct sunlight. Reconstitute only with the provided diluent, and use within 2 hours. Use clean syringes and boil them for 10 minutes before use. Never use disinfectants on syringes because they kill the vaccine. For Newcastle, you can also use a drinking water route, but add skim milk powder (2g per litre) to protect the virus. Withdraw water for 2 hours before giving the vaccine so birds are thirsty. Give enough waterers so every bird drinks. After vaccination, birds may look slightly sick for a day; that's normal. Keep records: date, vaccine name, batch number, and number of birds. In many African countries, the government or NGOs provide free ND vaccines. Contact your local veterinary office. If you cannot afford all vaccines, prioritize Newcastle because it kills fastest. Never vaccinate sick birds; wait until they recover. A good protocol can save 90% of your flock from deadly outbreaks.

lessons.title: Parasite Control
lessons.body: Parasites are silent thieves that steal your turkeys' feed and health. The two main types are internal (worms) and external (lice, mites, fleas). Internal worms like roundworms and tapeworms cause weight loss, dull feathers, and diarrhea. You can deworm every 3 months with levamisole or albendazole. Give the correct dose: usually 1 ml per 5 kg body weight orally. For a 10 kg turkey, give 2 ml. Use a syringe without needle and squirt into the beak. After deworming, collect and burn droppings for 24 hours to prevent reinfection. For external parasites, check under wings and around the vent. Lice and mites cause itching, feather loss, and restlessness. Dust birds with permethrin powder or spray with a solution of 2 ml permethrin per litre of water. Treat the house too: spray walls, roosts, and floor. Repeat after 10 days to kill newly hatched eggs. Keep litter dry; wet litter breeds coccidia and flies. Use wood shavings or chopped straw, and stir it daily. Add diatomaceous earth to dust baths; it cuts parasites naturally. Rotate your turkeys to fresh pasture if you free-range, and don't overcrowd. For coccidiosis, use amprolium in water for 5 days as a treatment, and consider a coccidiostat in feed for prevention. In Africa, many farmers use local plants like neem or tobacco leaves as repellents, but these are not as reliable as modern dewormers. Always follow withdrawal periods: for meat, stop dewormers 14 days before slaughter. Keep a deworming calendar and stick to it. Healthy turkeys gain weight faster and lay more eggs.

lessons.title: Biosecurity Practices
lessons.body: Biosecurity means keeping germs out of your turkey farm. It is the cheapest way to prevent disease. Start with a fence around your compound to keep out wild birds and visitors. Wild birds carry Newcastle and avian influenza. Use a footbath at the entrance of each pen. Fill it with 2% sodium hypochlorite (bleach) or 1% formalin. Change the solution daily. Only you and essential workers should enter. Wear dedicated boots and overalls that you leave at the farm. Never wear the same clothes to the market and then to your turkeys. Keep turkeys away from chickens, ducks, and other poultry. Chickens carry blackhead and coccidia without getting sick. If you must keep both, house them in separate buildings at least 50 metres apart. Quarantine new birds for 3 weeks in a separate pen. Watch for signs of illness before mixing. Clean and disinfect feeders and drinkers daily. Use a brush and soap, then rinse with bleach solution. Store feed in sealed containers to keep out rats and wild birds. Rats carry salmonella and leptospirosis. Control rodents with traps, not poison, because turkeys may eat poisoned rats. Remove dead birds immediately. Burn or bury them 1 metre deep with lime. Compost manure away from the turkey house. Limit visitors; if they must come, give them boots and a coat. After handling birds, wash your hands with soap. If you visit another farm, change clothes and shower before returning to your turkeys. These steps reduce disease risk by over 90%. Good biosecurity saves money on drugs and prevents heartbreak.

lessons.title: Recognizing Sick Birds
lessons.body: You must spot sick turkeys early to save them and the flock. A healthy turkey is alert, active, and has bright eyes and red wattles. It eats and drinks well, and its droppings are firm with a white cap. A sick turkey often stands apart with drooped wings and a dull, pale head. It may close its eyes or have a runny nose. Check for these signs every morning and evening. Look at the droppings: green or yellow watery droppings mean infection; bloody droppings mean coccidiosis; white pasty droppings mean pullorum. Listen for sneezing, coughing, or rattling breath. Watch for head shaking or twisting of the neck, which suggests Newcastle. Check the legs and feet for swelling or scabs, a sign of fowl pox or bumblefoot. Feel the crop: if it is hard and full, the bird may have impacted crop; if it is soft and squishy, it may have sour crop. A sick bird often stops eating but may drink a lot. Take its temperature if you can; normal is 40-41Â°C. If you find a sick bird, isolate it immediately in a warm, quiet pen. Give it clean water with electrolytes and vitamins. Do not medicate blindly; call a vet or extension officer. If the bird dies, do not eat it. Send the body to a lab if possible for diagnosis. Keep a notebook to record symptoms, dates, and treatments. Over time, you will learn to spot problems before they spread. In Africa, where vet access is limited, your eyes are your best tool. Early action saves the flock.

lessons.title: Working with Veterinarians
lessons.body: A good veterinarian is your best partner in turkey farming. In many African countries, you can find vets through the Ministry of Agriculture, veterinary schools, or private clinics. Some also work for NGOs. Start by building a relationship before you have an emergency. Invite a vet to visit your farm once a year for a health check. That way, when disease strikes, they know your setup. Keep a record book with all treatments, vaccinations, and deaths. This helps the vet make a quick diagnosis. When you call a vet, describe the symptoms clearly: how many birds are sick, their age, what you see in droppings, and when it started. If the vet cannot come, you can send photos or short videos via WhatsApp. Many vets now offer phone consultations. For laboratory tests, collect fresh droppings or a dead bird in a plastic bag on ice. Do not freeze. The vet may prescribe antibiotics, dewormers, or vaccines. Always follow the dosage and withdrawal period. Never buy drugs from unlicensed sellers; they may be fake. If you cannot afford a private vet, contact your local government veterinary officer. They often provide free or subsidized services. Some African countries have community animal health workers who can help with basic treatments. Attend farmer field days and workshops where vets teach. Learn to give injections yourself for simple cases, but always ask for guidance first. A vet can also help you design a vaccination schedule and biosecurity plan. Remember, vets are busy; be polite and pay promptly if private. Good vet relationships lead to healthier flocks and higher profits.

quiz.q: Which disease causes twisting of the neck in turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle disease often causes nervous signs like twisted neck.

quiz.q: What is the main sign of blackhead disease?
options: B) Yellow droppings and dark head
quiz.explanation: Blackhead causes yellow droppings and a darkening of the head.

quiz.q: Which parasite causes coccidiosis?
quiz.explanation: Coccidiosis is caused by protozoan parasites called coccidia.

quiz.q: What is the treatment for coccidiosis?
quiz.explanation: Amprolium is the standard treatment for coccidiosis.

quiz.q: Why should turkeys not be kept with chickens?
options: B) Chickens carry blackhead without getting sick
quiz.explanation: Chickens are carriers of the blackhead parasite, which is deadly to turkeys.

quiz.q: At what age should poults receive their first Newcastle vaccine?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle vaccine is given as early as day 1 via eye or nostril drop.

quiz.q: How should vaccines be stored?
options: A) In a cool, dark place with ice packs
quiz.explanation: Vaccines must be kept cool, not frozen, and away from sunlight.

quiz.q: What is added to drinking water when giving Newcastle vaccine orally?
quiz.explanation: Skim milk powder protects the vaccine virus in water.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Deworming every 3 months is a common recommendation.

quiz.q: Which drug is used to deworm turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Levamisole is an effective dewormer for poultry.

quiz.q: What is the correct dose of levamisole for a 10 kg turkey?
quiz.explanation: The dose is 1 ml per 5 kg, so a 10 kg turkey gets 2 ml.

quiz.q: How do you treat external parasites like lice?
quiz.explanation: Permethrin powder or spray kills lice and mites.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for dewormers before slaughter?
quiz.explanation: A 14-day withdrawal ensures no drug residues in meat.

quiz.q: What is the first step in biosecurity?
quiz.explanation: A fence keeps out wild birds and unwanted visitors.

quiz.q: What should be used in a footbath?
quiz.explanation: A 2% sodium hypochlorite (bleach) solution disinfects boots.

quiz.q: How long should new birds be quarantined?
quiz.explanation: A 3-week quarantine allows time for diseases to show.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid poison for rat control?
options: B) Turkeys may eat poisoned rats
quiz.explanation: Turkeys can get secondary poisoning from eating poisoned rodents.

quiz.q: How deep should you bury dead birds?
quiz.explanation: Burying 1 metre deep with lime prevents disease spread.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a healthy turkey?
options: B) Bright eyes and red wattles
quiz.explanation: Bright eyes and red wattles indicate good health.

quiz.q: What do bloody droppings indicate?
quiz.explanation: Bloody droppings are a classic sign of coccidiosis.

quiz.q: What is the normal body temperature of a turkey?
quiz.explanation: Turkeys normally have a body temperature of 40-41Â°C.

quiz.q: What should you do first when you find a sick bird?
quiz.explanation: Isolation prevents the spread of disease to healthy birds.

quiz.q: Why should you not eat a bird that died from disease?
options: B) It may carry toxins or pathogens
quiz.explanation: Dead birds may harbor harmful bacteria or toxins.

quiz.q: How can you find a veterinarian in Africa?
options: A) Through the Ministry of Agriculture
quiz.explanation: Government veterinary offices are a reliable source.

quiz.q: What should you record in your farm notebook?
quiz.explanation: Records of vaccinations and treatments help vets diagnose.

quiz.q: What is a sign of fowl pox?
options: A) Scabs on head and legs
quiz.explanation: Fowl pox causes scabs on unfeathered areas.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is given by wing web stab?
quiz.explanation: Fowl pox vaccine is administered by pricking the wing web.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent Newcastle disease?
quiz.explanation: There is no cure for Newcastle, so vaccination is key.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cannot afford all vaccines?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle is the most deadly, so prioritize it.

quiz.q: What is a good practice after handling birds?
quiz.explanation: Washing hands prevents spreading pathogens.
